{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=automated+hypothesis+falsification+and+self-reflection+in+AI+scientific+agents&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"A Peircean framework for explainable and human-centred artificial intelligence\", \"abstract\": null, \"doi\": null, \"pmid\": \"PMC13658564\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13658564\", \"source\": \"PMC\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"PubMedCentral\", \"url\": \"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13658564/?tool=EBI\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"PubMedCentral\", \"url\": \"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13658564/pdf/?tool=EBI\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13658564\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13658564?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"From information to existence: the Information-Meaning-Existence (IBE) framework as a meta-method for second-order observation.\", \"abstract\": \"Sociological systems theory offers a rich vocabulary for meaning, observation, and communication, but that vocabulary has proven difficult to translate into executable, testable, and revisable procedures. This gap has become more consequential as large language models are increasingly used to read, summarize, and simulate social-scientific discourse without any shared standard for distinguishing genuine semantic stabilization from fluent but ungrounded continuation. This paper introduces the Information-Meaning-Existence (IBE) framework, which reconstructs Luhmannian second-order observation as a validation architecture. A coherence index tracks whether actualized meaning-relations remain viable as their context changes, and a companion diagnostic identifies when that viability collapses-distinguishing collapse as failure from collapse as a precondition for new distinctions. The framework specifies how its central quantities could be computed from text using existing embedding-based and information-theoretic methods, disambiguates several senses in which a meaning-structure can be said to \\\"exist,\\\" and extends the coherence index to register cases in which apparent stability is sustained by structural power rather than genuine resonance. A concluding discussion confronts this coherence-centered vocabulary with dialectical accounts of development in which contradiction, not coherence, drives change, and uses that confrontation to recalibrate the framework's own claims. The paper specifies what an empirical pilot would require to calibrate and test the framework, and explicitly states that absent such calibration, its present status is proto-scientific.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fsoc.2026.1871301\", \"pmid\": \"42761487\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13587620\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fsoc.2026.1871301\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13587620\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13587620?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Autonomous artificial intelligence, scientific research, and human values.\", \"abstract\": \"During the initial stage of AI's incorporation into scientific research, AI systems have functioned predominantly as tools under direct human supervision and control. However, AI incorporation into scientific research is now entering a stage in which AI Agents perform research tasks with partial autonomy while remaining under human supervision and control. In the not-too-distant future, a third stage may arise when autonomous AI systems conduct their own research and generate knowledge without human supervision or control. While the second and third stages of AI-augmented research may offer substantial benefits for science and society, they also create novel ethical issues, including (1) Conducting immoral research that may harm humans and other forms of life; (2) Increasing rate of biased, erroneous and deceptive research; (3) Confidentiality challenges; (4) Overreliance on AI; (5) Diffusion of responsibility and accountability; (6) Deskilling; (7) Job losses; (8) AI-generated research beyond human comprehension; and (9) Erosion of trust. We suggest specific solutions to minimize the negative consequences of these issues and offer proposals for ensuring that incorporation of AI into scientific research supports human values.\", \"doi\": \"10.1007/s43681-025-00908-0\", \"pmid\": \"41768290\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC12948163\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00908-0\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12948163\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12948163?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Ideometrics: a scientific approach to generating, evaluating, and prioritising ideas.\", \"abstract\": \"

Background

This paper introduces and describes a new integrative scientific approach - ideometrics - building on the 'sense of ideas' and 'value of information' concepts. Ideometrics is the emerging field of generating, evaluating, and prioritising ideas.

Methods

Focused on the generation, evaluation and prioritisation of ideas, we identified and then mapped the landscape of methodological approaches that have been used over time, disciplines, and epistemic paradigms across many areas of human enquiry. Although these often appeared to arise independently, isolated by geographical and disciplinary boundaries, they share remarkable conceptual and structural similarities, from creative ideation, balancing of subjective and objective criteria, to iterative refinement. Finally, we sought to integrate these traditions through an empirical scientific framework.

Results

We identified over 70 different methodological approaches. We then proposed several steps to establish ideometrics as a rigorous and practically useful field of science, rather than merely an integrative framework. Ideometrics is falsifiable: it supports testable predictions about future performance of competing ideas, while its methods are increasingly evolving into rigorous, structured, standardised and mathematically characterised tools. It enables accumulation of evidence and progressive refinement of theory, application of statistical inference, and introduction of artificial intelligence (AI).

Conclusions

Future progress will make ideometrics increasingly quantitative, digital, testable and replicable. We therefore foresee assessments of scientific footprints of each of the >70 methodological approaches, developing formal reporting guidelines to standardise ideometrics studies and allow meta-analyses, and conducting empirical comparisons between methods used to address the same challenges. Ideometrics represents an attempt to systematically unify the scientific approaches to generating, evaluating, and prioritising ideas. Its practical application should address scarcity by assisting individuals, institutions, and societies to focus their limited time, energy, capacity and resources on pursuing the ideas that are most likely to achieve their stated aims, based on an objective and scientific approach, rather than subjective and intuitive priority setting.\", \"doi\": \"10.7189/jogh.15.04360\", \"pmid\": \"41685986\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC12904029\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.15.04360\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12904029\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12904029?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "0634e36e927fcec6c1b08f53bed756fa50cabca07c8114bb16f1e951b14e3b44", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.3389/fsoc.2026.1871301", "doi:10.1007/s43681-025-00908-0", "doi:10.7189/jogh.15.04360", "pmc:PMC13658564", "pmc:PMC13587620", "pmc:PMC12948163", "pmc:PMC12904029"], "source_candidates": ["https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13658564/?tool=EBI", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13658564/pdf/?tool=EBI", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13658564", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13658564?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3389/fsoc.2026.1871301", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13587620", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13587620?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00908-0"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

article.body:
Consider a chef who tastes a dish mid-recipe to decide whether to add more salt or start over entirely. As an analogy, computer workers examine how artificial systems monitor their own choices during complex tasks. Our group is investigating how these systems allocate their mental effort between planning and execution. [1]

Team members 100, 101, 102, and 103 analyzed how reasoning models handle external oversight and multi-turn problems. Their recorded readings indicate that metareasoning governs how resources are split between planning and action. Paper-supported notes suggest that multi-turn models show distinct behavioral shifts under external supervision, while autonomous frameworks require self-generated goals to acquire flexible skills. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Meanwhile, teams 200, 201, 202, and 203 looked into epistemic self-correction and preference formation. Their findings highlight that inferential errors during preference updates are often path-dependent under misspecified models. Furthermore, recorded reviews emphasize that intrinsic self-correction remains fundamentally limited without external validation signals. [5, 6, 7, 8]

Rounding out the group, teams 300, 301, 302, and 303 explored curiosity-driven learning and multi-agent coordination. Their notebook records note that curiosity-driven strategies help agents explore complex problems with rare rewards, while structured communication dimensions improve joint performance across multiple units. [9, 10, 11, 12]

How can explicit falsification mechanisms be generalized across more diverse, unconstrained scientific domains when intrinsic correction falls short? [5]

Summary

We study how computer systems examine their reasoning using published papers. We look at resource management, preferences, and self-correction limits. We still do not know if systems can truly question their starting rules. We follow the Console as new readings arrive.
article.lede: We continue exploring how computer systems examine their own reasoning, tracking the shift from rigid calculations to flexible self-evaluation.
article.lens: Investigating the boundaries of automated reflection through shared source readings and safety frameworks.
article.title: Mapping the Machinery of Machine Reflection
